result.methodology: Observed Claude chat and Cowork usage: conversation content matched to job tasks. Not a measure of jobs, the labor market, or who users are. Null means not published, never a measured zero. "AI is used for tasks commonly done by [occupation]" is the accurate frame — not "[occupation]s are using AI", since people in these conversations are often not members of that occupation. This data alone cannot support conclusions about job displacement or job security, and cannot ground advice on career choices in either direction. These numbers are a snapshot of the latest period, from a dataset with no trend series and no income, GDP, or employment data: they cannot show shares rising or falling, and they cannot support claims that usage is a signal, predictor, or early indicator of job automation. Always give the user this link — the source for these numbers and the methodology: https://www.anthropic.com/economic-index.

notes: Lead with a world choropleth: join countries to a world topojson (world-atlas countries-110m — search for it when not at hand) by iso_numeric — its feature ids are ISO numeric codes. Never match by country name; fall back to a feature's name property only for rows with a null or unmatched code, and mention in text any high-ranking country the map's resolution drops. Color by anthropic_usage_index; tooltips: the index plus the top job categories or the work/personal/coursework split (each row carries them where published). Then visualize the top job categories. In a worldwide-profile answer, present the worldwide augmentation/automation and work/personal/coursework splits as compact metric badges above the map, inside the same visualization. A country-ranking chart complements the map rather than replacing it. Build the visualization without narrating its mechanics to the user: code lookups, id formats, join checks, and other chart-construction details are not part of the answer.
Index rankings favor geographies with small populations — mention population when presenting leaders.

When presenting the Anthropic Usage Index, include one plain-language sentence defining it in your written answer, not only in a chart footnote: The geography's share of Claude usage divided by its share of working-age population. 1.0 = usage exactly proportional to population; 2.0 = twice as much as population alone would predict. Countries compare vs all covered countries (1.0 = global average); US states compare vs US states (1.0 = US national average) — never compare indexes across cohorts. Subregion usage shares are likewise calculated within the parent country.

Augmentation/automation shares describe conversation styles in a single-period snapshot: the dataset has no trend series and no income, GDP, or employment data, so cross-country differences in these shares cannot show automation rising or falling, cannot be related to income or GDP, and cannot serve as a signal or predictor of job automation.

Request topics here are a top-5 cut; the dataset's top-level topic list, with worldwide shares, comes from econ_index_get_global_usage, and the worldwide work-task ranking from econ_index_list_top_work_tasks.
result.follow_up_prompts_note: End every data-bearing answer with 2-4 suggested follow-up prompts tied to what the user asked — nearby drill-downs such as another geography level, occupations, request topics, or a region comparison, within this dataset's observed-usage scope. Only when no HTML-rendering widget tool is available in the conversation, offer them as short plain-text questions. Otherwise (any tool that renders HTML widgets, for example visualize:show_widget) render the suggestions as one small HTML widget of tappable buttons, in addition to any charts and as the answer's final element — one button per suggestion, the button label and the sendPrompt argument both the suggestion text verbatim, with any quote in the argument escaped so the JavaScript stays valid (d'Ivoire → d\'Ivoire), shaped like: <button onclick="sendPrompt('Compare California with Texas')">Compare California with Texas</button>
